title: Baseline change and detail change
blurb: Decide whether a change alters the project baseline or is a detail change, and say who handles each and how.
question: Users ask for a new Must have feature that would add an epic to the agreed project backlog. Can the team simply trade it in, or must it be decided formally, and by whom?

teach.body: In PRINCE2 Agile, the key question for any new or changed requirement is whether it changes the agreed project backlog. If it does, for example a new Must have epic, it is a change to the project baseline: it needs formal handling and is decided by the project board, or by whoever holds delegated authority to decide on changes. If it does not, it is a detail change: it is handled informally at team level, by the team and product owner.

children.edge: Leaves the project backlog as it is
children.label: Detail change

teach.h: Detail change is welcome, not a threat
teach.body: A request that does not affect the project backlog is seen as making the final product more accurate, so it is viewed as something positive. That does not mean it is simply added on top. The product owner and team prioritize it, and if it ranks above existing work, they trade it in for lower-priority items of similar effort, so the iteration and overall scope stay balanced. It should not be ignored.

head: Artifact
Holds
Owner
teach.caption: Changes to the project backlog go formal; changes below it stay at team level.

teach.h: A Must have label is no shortcut
teach.body: A team may feel a new requirement is a Must have and want to add it at once. If it changes the project backlog, it is still a baseline change and still needs a formal decision at the right management level, however important it seems. Equally, a change that stays inside the agreed baseline does not need the board, even if it is time-consuming to discuss. The deciding factor is the effect on the baseline.

teach.h: Formal route for a baseline change

teach.body: Project manager Owen Pritchard runs an agile project for a mortgage app. Users ask for clearer wording on the affordability screen, a story already in the product backlog: a detail change, so product owner Lena Fischer reprioritizes it and swaps out a story of similar effort. Then the marketing director asks for a new buy-to-let journey as a Must have, which would add an epic to the agreed project backlog. That is a baseline change, so Owen raises an issue report and the project board decides.

teach.h: A nuance from the official samples
teach.body: In one official practitioner rationale, a low-priority Could-have that fitted within the planned timeframe was added to the project backlog without needing a decision from the chief product owner, and was not treated as a baseline change. The same rationale notes that any cost effects could be absorbed by trading lower-priority Could-haves. Because the official samples do not settle how every Could-have addition is treated, rely on the safe core rule: a change to Must haves or other approved scope in the project backlog goes formal.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.3.2 (as quoted in the V2 sample rationales)

teach.text: Trading is for detail changes inside the baseline. A change that alters the project backlog cannot be traded away at team level, and the Agilometer plays no part in deciding it: it is a risk tool for agile working.

items: Changes the project backlog = baseline change: formal, decided by the board or delegated change authority (11.3.2).
Does not change the project backlog = detail change: informal, at team level with the PO.
Detail change is seen as positive: a more accurate final product.
Detail changes are prioritized and traded, not ignored.
A Must have label never lets the team skip the formal route for a baseline change.

summary: You can now decide whether a change is a baseline change or a detail change by asking whether it alters the project backlog. You can also say that baseline changes go formally to the board or change authority, while detail changes are handled by the team and product owner.

A.q: A new Must have requirement means the agreed project backlog would have to change. How is this treated?
options: As a detail change, traded in by the team
As a risk to log in the risk register
As an off-specification for the tester
As a change to the project baseline
A.why: A new Must have that means the agreed project backlog must change is a change to the project baseline, handled formally (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Detail changes leave the project backlog unchanged; this one alters it.
whyNot.1: A requested change has already arisen, so it is an issue, not an uncertain risk.
whyNot.2: Nothing has failed its quality specification; this is a change in requirements.

A.q: Who decides on a change that affects the project baseline?
options: The product owner together with the delivery team
The team coach, at the next team retrospective workshop
The board or those with delegated change authority
The project manager, at the next daily stand-up meeting
A.why: Baseline changes need formal handling and are decided by the project board, or by the person or persons given authority to decide on changes (11.3.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.0: The PO and team handle detail changes that leave the baseline unchanged.
whyNot.1: The team coach supports self-management; it does not decide baseline changes.
whyNot.3: Baseline decisions sit at the appropriate management level, not in a stand-up.

A.q: How is a detail change viewed in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: As making the final product more accurate
As a threat to be escalated to the board
As scope creep to be refused by the PO
As a reason to raise an exception report
A.why: A change that does not affect the project backlog is seen as creating a more accurate final product, and so as positive (11.3.2).

whyNot.1: Detail changes are handled at team level; escalation is for baseline changes.
whyNot.2: Detail changes are prioritized and possibly traded in, not refused as scope creep.
whyNot.3: An exception report is for a forecast breach of tolerance, not a detail change.

B.q: Users ask to reword a confirmation message on a story already in the product backlog. The project backlog is unaffected. How is this handled?
options: Formally, through an issue report to the board
By the change authority at the next stage boundary
Informally, at team level with the product owner
By the CPO, who rewrites the project backlog
B.why: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Formal handling with an issue report is for baseline changes.
whyNot.1: Change authority decisions concern baseline changes, not wording inside a story.
whyNot.3: The project backlog is unaffected, so the CPO has nothing to change there.

B.q: A team labels a new requirement as a Must have, but adding it would add an epic to the project backlog. What should happen?
options: The team adds it at once because it is a Must have
The team swaps it for a Could have of equal effort
The tester logs it as an off-specification
It is handled formally as a change to the baseline
B.why: It alters the project backlog, so it is a baseline change needing formal handling by the board or change authority, whatever its priority label (11.3.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.0: The MoSCoW label does not let the team bypass a baseline decision.
whyNot.1: Trading is for detail changes inside the baseline, not changes that alter the project backlog.
whyNot.2: No product has missed its quality specification; this is a new requirement.

B.q:
Which two statements about changes in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Detail changes are set aside so the iteration is protected.
2. A new Must have that alters the project backlog is a baseline change.
3. Detail changes are handled informally at team level.
4. Baseline changes can be traded in by the team without the board.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 3
1 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: A new Must have that alters the project backlog is a baseline change (2), and detail changes are handled informally at team level (3) (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is wrong: detail changes are prioritized and traded, not set aside.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: detail changes are not set aside, and baseline changes need a formal decision.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: baseline changes are decided formally at management level.

C.q: Whether a change is a baseline change depends on its effect on which artifact, and who owns that artifact?
options: Product backlog; the product owner
Release map; the project manager
Team plan; the team coach
Project backlog; chief product owner
C.why: A change that alters the project backlog is a baseline change (11.3.2), and the CPO owns the project backlog (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: Changes within a product backlog that leave the project backlog intact are detail changes; the PO owns the product backlog.
whyNot.1: The release map is the plan; the baseline test in 11.3.2 is the project backlog.
whyNot.2: The team plan holds iteration tasks; the team coach does not own a baseline artifact.

C.q: A detail change arrives that ranks above an existing story in the current iteration. What should the team do?
options: Raise an exception report to the project board
Trade it for a lower-priority item of similar effort
Add it on top and extend the iteration by a week
Record it in the risk register for next stage
C.why: Detail changes are prioritized and, if higher priority, traded for lower-priority work of similar effort, agreed with the PO (11.3.2, 11.4.1).

whyNot.0: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so an exception report is not needed.
whyNot.2: Timeboxes are fixed, and adding work on top grows scope; trading keeps it balanced.
whyNot.3: It is a change that has arisen, not an uncertainty, and it can be handled now.

C.q: Which management product describes a baseline change's impacts, options and recommendation for the decision maker?
options: Issue report
Highlight report
Exception report
Lessons report
C.why: An issue report describes the issue's impacts on the project baseline, identifies ways to resolve it and recommends a decision (Table 11.1).

whyNot.1: A highlight report, or project dashboard, gives regular status to the board.
whyNot.2: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance.
whyNot.3: A lessons report passes on lessons to embed in ways of working.

reteach.title: Rearranging the furniture or building an extension
reteach.question: How is the difference between a detail change and a baseline change like work on a house?

blocks.h: Inside the walls or outside them
blocks.body: Moving furniture around inside your house needs no permission: you decide with your family. Building an extension changes the agreed plans, so it goes to the planning committee. The project backlog is the agreed plan of the house. Rearranging stories inside it is a detail change for the team and product owner. Adding a new Must have epic changes the plan itself, so the board or change authority decides.

blocks.text: Ask one question: does it change the project backlog? Yes = formal. No = team level.

explain.body: If a new or changed requirement means the project backlog must change, it is a change to the project baseline.

test.q: Which artifact's change marks a change to the project baseline in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: The team plan
The product backlog
The project backlog
The team dashboard
test.why: A change that alters the project backlog is a change to the project baseline (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: The team plan changes every iteration as part of normal team planning.
whyNot.1: Changes within a product backlog that leave the project backlog intact are detail changes.
whyNot.3: The team dashboard shows progress; it is not the baseline.

explain.body: Baseline changes need formal handling and are decided by the project board or by those with delegated authority to decide on changes.

test.q: How must a change to the project baseline be handled?
options: Informally by the team and product owner
Formally at the appropriate management level
Through swarming by the whole delivery team
Through the next team retrospective workshop
test.why: Issues with an impact on the baseline must be handled and decided formally at the appropriate management level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Informal team handling is for detail changes.
whyNot.2: Swarming resolves blockers; it does not decide baseline changes.
whyNot.3: Retrospectives look back on an iteration; they do not decide baseline changes.

explain.body: A change that leaves the project backlog unchanged is handled informally at team level. It is seen as positive: a more accurate final product.

test.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A change that does not affect the project backlog is a [?] change.
options: baseline
formal
detail
scope
test.why: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: A baseline change is one that alters the project backlog.
whyNot.1: Formal handling applies to baseline changes.
whyNot.3: Scope is a performance aspect, not the name of this kind of change.

explain.body: Even a Must have goes formal if it alters the project backlog. The effect on the baseline decides the route, not the priority.

test.q: What decides whether a change is handled formally or at team level?
options: Whether it affects the agreed project baseline
Whether the team rates it as a Must have
Whether the tester raised it during testing
Whether it arrived in the current iteration
test.why: Issues that affect the baseline go formal; those that do not are handled informally at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.1: A Must have that alters the project backlog still needs a formal decision.
whyNot.2: Who raises an issue does not decide its route.
whyNot.3: Timing does not decide the route; the effect on the baseline does.
